title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services

reading.body:
AI-generated video and fake social media profiles were used to impersonate a named, real immigration attorney, Angel Leal, across TikTok, Facebook, and Instagram. Scammers used his likeness to advertise fraudulent immigration services, directed victims to WhatsApp for fake contracts, and collected payment through digital payment apps. The operation was large enough that nearly 6,500 accounts had to be removed across three platforms before reporting occurred.

The failure mode here is impersonation enabled by generative AI, deployed entirely outside any legitimate system and without any platform-level check that caught it at scale before harm occurred. The platforms did remove accounts when identified, but the volume, nearly 6,500 fake profiles, indicates detection lagged far behind creation. Catching this earlier would have required either faster automated detection of synthetic video tied to a real person's identity or proactive monitoring by the platforms themselves, neither of which operated effectively here.

What is not established is who the scammers are, where they are located, or whether any law enforcement action has produced findings, as reporting describes only that Leal planned to contact authorities.

reports.title: Scammers steal identity of renowned Miami attorney to target immigrants on social media
South Florida immigration attorney says AI scammers are using his identity to target immigrants
Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
Legal resident loses thousands seeking citizenship to AI immigration attorney

summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become the target of an extensive artificial intelligence scam targeting vulnerable immigrants. Criminals have created hundreds of fake social media profiles and AI-generated videos depicting Leal offering fraudulent immigration services, including false claims about obtaining US residency for $2,200. The scams began escalating dramatically in recent months after Leal's office first noticed suspicious activity last October. His anti-piracy team has successfully removed nearly 6,500 fake accounts, including 3,500 from TikTok, 2,400 from Facebook, and 544 from Instagram.

The scammers typically direct victims through social media videos to contact phone numbers via WhatsApp, where they send fake contracts and request payments through digital payment apps like Venmo and Zelle. Fake testimonials claim that supposed former clients received legal status through Leal's help. Leal warns immigrants to verify the identity of legal service providers online and avoid sending money immediately through payment apps. He has changed his personal phone number and plans to contact local and federal authorities this week to investigate the source of the fraud.
